(Invocation) I bow to the beautiful, auspicious Light, which destroys the darkness of ignorance, illuminates the knowledge of reality, and bestows all desired objects. 1.

I bow to that father who has seen the further shore of the ocean of the Vedas and Shastras, who is exceedingly skillful in the performance of rituals such as sacrifices, and whose mind is purified by the worship of Sadashiva. // 2 //

Having prostrated before the venerable Śrī Khaṇḍadeva, my true guru, who is the sun to the lotus-heart of the Mīmāṃsakas, I compose this commentary, the *Prabhāvalī*, upon his work which treats the categories in an extremely concise manner. (3)
Even though some points have been raised here by me regarding what has already been composed by the Guru, this is not an act of malice on my part, for I am skilled in promoting [the teachings].

Rather, my intention is this: may those ornaments of the earth, whose intellects are as sharp as kusa-grass tips and who hold firm devotion to the established tenets, set aside my words and instead adorn his work.
(Commencement of the *Ṭippaṇa*: Declaration of Intent) Furthermore,

although the *Bhaṭṭadīpikā* has its meaning explained by my own work, the *Kaustubha*, up until the conclusion of the section on relative strength (*balābala*), it was the command of my venerable preceptors that I should compose this *Ṭippaṇa* while omitting that portion.
It is not appropriate to compose a commentary on that concluding section;

nevertheless, following the very path shown by the Kaustubha, a commentary is commenced from the beginning for the benefit of the world and to demonstrate that the meanings summarized therein are grounded in the words of the original text. (The promise of the introductory investigation)

In this regard, within the section concerning the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that will be explained, certain preliminary matters required as an introduction are first examined. To begin with, in the preceding section, it was stated: "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*). *Jaimini Sūtra* 1.1.1.

Thus, by means of this opening sūtra of the treatise, the great sage Jaimini has declared the entire subject matter of the śāstra— which consists of the objects of knowledge such as dharma and adharma— to be investigated through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), their nature, their instruments, and their results, along with their fallacies.
(This establishes the necessity of the investigation.)
And the root of the commencement of this treatise is the injunction for study: "One's own Veda is to be studied" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.15).

Since the knowledge of the meaning does not arise without inquiry due to the prescription of the act of study as the instrument (*karaṇa*), there follows an implication (*ākṣepa*) for the performance of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consisting of inquiry.

Because that [duty] must be performed, and because such performance is impossible in the absence of a scripture that teaches it, there is also an implicit injunction of the result—which consists in the understanding of the duty to begin the scripture and to study it.
As it has been said:
"When dharma is being cognized by means of the Veda acting as the instrument..."
"The portion concerning the 'how-to' (itikartavyatā) will be fulfilled by Mīmāṃsā."

(B3) (1) F.N.— In this introductory section, although they have promised that the commentary (*ṭippaṇa*) will begin by first determining the meaning of the sūtras starting with "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) and then summarizing the subject matter of the first chapter independently, they nevertheless compose the commentary starting precisely from the chapter on *arthavāda*.
The venerable Śambhubhaṭṭas maintain that the commentary on the first pāda of the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* composed by Ācārya Khaṇḍadeva is non-existent;

however, it is observed that the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* for the first pāda has been published in the edition of the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* printed in the city of Mysore, and furthermore, a commentary on the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* of the first pāda titled *Bhāṭṭakalpataru*, following that very work, is also available from the esteemed and highly respected Mahāmahopādhyāyas, the illustrious Rāmasubrahmaṇya Śāstrins.
Regarding this, many believe that the *Bhaṭṭadīpikā* composed by someone else as an independent work is indeed that [text], and not the one authored by Ācārya Khaṇḍadeva.
The fact that the edition of the *Bhaṭṭadīpikā* printed in Calcutta begins from the second pāda [of the first adhyāya] also supports their view.

Furthermore, the *Mantrādhikaraṇa* and the sections on the definitions of injunctions such as *niyama* and *parisaṃkhyā*, which are found in the Calcutta edition of the *Bhaṭṭadīpikā*, [are likewise absent in Khaṇḍadeva’s work].

They describe it as follows: "This [text], measuring only one folio (*ekapuṭa*), was found by us even among those ancient palm-leaf manuscripts that we have discovered; having been extracted from the first quarter (*pāda*) while being found in the *Mantrādhikaraṇa*, it was published by someone.
In this regard, one might ask: was it extracted from the first quarter and then incorporated into the *Mantrādhikaraṇa*?

Furthermore, the doubt that [the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*] might begin from the first section on Mantras (*mantrādhikaraṇa*) finds no occasion here; for it is observed that the commentary of Śambhubhaṭṭa—the former student of Khaṇḍadevācārya’s beloved disciple Priya—begins precisely at that *mantrādhikaraṇa*. Moreover, as for those other portions where the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* was composed by Khaṇḍadevācārya starting only from the second section (*dvitīyapāda*), [the same applies].

Regarding the first pāda, however, the reasons for the claim that this *Bhaṭṭadīpikā* printed in the city of Mysore is a different work— composed either by some modern or ancient individual through the independent construction of various sentences while adopting the words of Khaṇḍadevācārya— are those which they hold as their own convictions.
We shall indicate those [details] in the introduction (*bhūmikā*) to this very work when it is published; therefore, we desist for fear of prolixity.

(B2) [Furthermore, regarding the intended sequence following study: Consequently, through the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅgavedādhyayana*), there results the knowledge of categories (*padārthajñāna*) consisting of the discernment of *dharma* and *adharma*, which is useful for the performance of rituals preceded by the study of the treatises on inquiry (*vicāraśāstra*).

In order to fulfill the established status of the injunction for study—which has a visible purpose—by the sense that "one should accomplish [the goal]," the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) consisting of non-interruption by other activities is also established for inquiry.
Even up to this point, the result of postulating such an intention is the sublation of the Smṛti rule: "Having studied, one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*)."

Otherwise, if one were to perform the *samāvartana* immediately after the study [of the Veda], it would follow that the study enjoined by the injunction for study has only an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose.

Even if the Smṛti were to establish that the cessation of all the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*)—characterized by the bath which signifies the end of those fixed rules—occurs immediately after study;
nevertheless, the contradiction [with the injunction for study] applies only to the aspect of returning from the teacher’s house (*gurukula*).
This is because that [prohibition] alone is incompatible with reflection (*vicāra*).

As it is stated in the *Vārttika*: "The cessation from the teacher's house, characterized by the student's ritual bath (*snāna*), would be sublated due to its incompatibility; however, the eating of honey and so forth would not."
"Therefore, one should remain in the teacher's house, avoiding honey, meat, and the like;
for it is understood that one should desire to know Dharma because it is not contradictory [to this]."

(On the performance of the *samāvartana* ceremony following the completion of Vedic study, and the refutation of the view that *samāvartana* occurs immediately after the investigation of ritual procedures:

Thus, even after the complete study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*), while still residing in the teacher’s house (*gurukula*), one may perform the *samāvartana*—which consists in the cessation of the other duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*)—and yet continue the study of the philosophical treatises (*vicāra-śāstra*) concerning dharma and adharma;

for there is no contradiction in the sense that the study of these treatises does not require the cessation of residence in the teacher’s house, nor does it imply the renunciation of everything immediately after such study.

Regarding the Smṛti rule concerning the performance of ritual action— namely, "Having studied, one should perform the ceremonial bath" (snāna)— this is established as referring merely to the time preceding the bath within the context of study; for, since the injunction to study can have the result of the comprehension of the visible meaning, it is improper to assume heaven [as its fruit], and because it is impossible to enjoin a sequence of immediate succession between study and the ceremonial bath (samāvartana).

Otherwise, because the instruction on the procedure for the meaning of the Veda at the conclusion of Vedic study— in the Taittirīya recension, by the passage beginning with "Having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the pupil" and ending with "In this manner you should conduct yourself toward them"— would be untenable,
it was argued that the inquiry into Dharma (dharmajijñāsā) alone is appropriate immediately after study, not the ceremonial bath (snāna); however, that [argument] has been refuted.

Because there would otherwise follow the denial of the investigation of the scriptures (*śāstravicāra*), which is established by the tradition of the learned (*śiṣṭasampradāya*) as being performed immediately after the *samāvartana*,

and because the fact that study (*adhyayana*) must precede the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) is already established by the force of the injunctions regarding the rules of initiation (*upanayana*), Vedic study (*adhyayana*), and studentship (*brahmacarya*); thus, the immediate succession of the act of study— which is not at all obtained among all the duties of a student (*brahmacārin*)— within the *samāvartana* [would be untenable].
Furthermore, because there would be no injunction [for such a sequence], it would result in the futility of the Smṛti rule, "Having studied, one should bathe" (*adhītya snāyāt*);

for even if the immediate succession between the study of the rules of recitation (*adhyayana-dharma*) and the inquiry (*vicāra*) were postulated in accordance with the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) of the injunction for study, such a sequence would remain untenable— since its visible purpose is not lost even when the inquiry into the scriptures begins immediately after the *samāvartana* on the very day the Vedic study is completed— therefore, [the sequence] of study and bathing...
Furthermore, there is no evidence for the sublation of the sequence;

for even according to you, since an interval is possible after the completion of Vedic study if a qualified teacher or other requisite is not found, and since sublation is necessary when there is no interval due to the performance of the mandatory worship of Gaṇapati and others, the understanding of mere immediate succession— by setting aside the aspect of non-interval— is intended to signify the cessation of other conflicting activities.
Since there is no contradiction in performing the *samāvartana* (the rite of returning home) as something fit for description, there is no sublation of that [obligation];
on the contrary, because activities such as wandering for alms (*bhikṣācarya*) are opposed to inquiry (*vicāra*), their cessation actually assists [the inquiry].

For this very reason, even when an obstructing factor exists, the commentators [Śrīkaṇṭha and others] have maintained in the *Śrutipadādyadhikaraṇa* that the sublation of the rule for bathing occurs by the force of the word *atha* itself, intending that the impossibility of study being the cause [of the next stage] arises from the abandonment of the aspect of "immediacy" (*avyavahitatva*).
It has been established.

Therefore, only that which is enjoined by the rule of bathing (*snāna-vidhi*)—namely, the cessation of residence in the teacher’s house (*gurukula-vāsa*)—must be set aside, since without it there would be a loss of the visible fruit (*dṛṣṭa-phala*) consisting of reflection (*vicāra*) as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) and the knowledge of meaning (*artha-jñāna*) resulting from the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*). And since that [cessation] is opposed to reflection, it is sublated by the injunction that prescribes immediate succession to study (*adhyayana-anantarya*).

However, it is a sound and faultless conception that there is no bathing at all—let alone one as powerful as the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana)—enjoined by an injunction as a constituent element of the rite apart from those [already mentioned].

Having taken as its very foundation this matter established both by the Vedic text and its meaning through the injunction for study, the Great Sage commenced his treatise with the aphorism: "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma."
(Description of the meaning of the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*):
The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: "Now" (*atha*) means immediately after the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-veda-adhyayana*).

For, by that [study] alone, without inquiry (*vicāra*), there does not arise a knowledge of the objects consisting of dharma and adharma—which takes the form of a determination useful for the performance [of rituals] and constitutes the fruit of that [study].
Therefore, because study has as its visible purpose the knowledge of meaning, the desire for such knowledge of dharma and adharma must be undertaken;
that is to say, such knowledge, which is the object of the desire, must be achieved.

And since that [knowledge] cannot be accomplished without inquiry, the meaning is that inquiry into it must be undertaken by means of the sources of knowledge (pramāṇa), their nature, their means of proof, and their results.
(Establishing the genitive compound *dharmajijñāsā* by determining the purpose through the intention to express the sense of "for the sake of" [tādarthya] in the phrase *dharmāya jijñāsā*):

Here, in the term *dharmajijñāsā*, the commentators and others have explained the genitive case as intending a specific relationship called "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*), namely *dharmāya jijñāsā*.

In this regard, setting aside the interpretation that takes the genitive to mean "object," the purpose of explaining it as signifying "being for the sake of" is precisely to make known that the inquiry is useful for the performance of dharma.
And thus, it follows by implication that this inquiry must be undertaken for the sake of the performance of dharma;
however, this is not intended to demonstrate a compound with the fourth case-ending (tādarthya-caturthī-samāsa).

For although such a compound might occasionally be possible according to the view of the Vārttikakāra—as in the case of words like *aśvaghāsa*—the Mahābhāṣyakāra rejected that view, since even in the word *aśvaghāsa* he resorts to a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

It is exactly so here as well, due to the propriety of that [interpretation]. For this very reason, the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda stated that the statement of the Commentator, "the desire to know for the sake of Dharma" (*dharmāya jijñāsā*), is intended to demonstrate the meaning obtained through a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), and not to demonstrate the actual analytical resolution (*vigraha*) of the compound itself.
In the scriptural statement "one would wish to know that," it has been explained through the analysis of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*);
therefore, it should be understood that the genitive compound alone is appropriate.
(Regarding the meaning of the term *jijñāsā*): In the word *jijñāsā*, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward "investigation" (*vicāra*).

Alternatively, since the necessity of investigation is established by the very sense of the words, there is no indication at all, according to the method stated in the Vārttika regarding the section beginning with the word *śruti*.
However, it should be understood that this refers precisely to what was heard [in the scripture].

(The purpose of the word *atha*): Furthermore, this sūtra uses the word *atha* to indicate that the inquiry [into Brahman] follows immediately after the study [of the Veda], which is established by the injunction for study; this is for the sake of establishing the sequence required by the sacred text (*śruti*).

For in cases where the sequence of immediate succession is established by the very order of recitation—as in the case of the portions to be cut from the heart and other organs—[the word *atha* serves to confirm it].

In this context, although the word "atha" (then/thereupon) functions as a restatement (*anuvāda*), since there is no injunction by a scriptural rule (*vidhi*) for two things already established by other means of knowledge, the word "atha" must serve to enjoin sequence (*krama*) in the form of immediate succession (*ānantarya*).

This is because, even in the present case, both study and inquiry are already established by the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) as being useful for the performance of ritual acts; therefore, it is understood that the word "atha" in the Sūtra is intended solely to enjoin the sequence.
And this has been indicated in the fifth [chapter] of both the Vārttika and the Tantraratna.

(An exposition, according to the opinion of some, that the subject matter of the inquiry into the *smṛtis* and so forth is also included within the scope of the initial proposition, by means of analyzing the view that the meaning of the Veda is the referent of the term *dharma*:

And in this regard— since it is stated that an inquiry must be undertaken immediately after the study of the Veda solely for the purpose of knowing the meaning of the Veda, the meaning of the Veda is to be desired to be known precisely as the "meaning of the Veda," and not as "dharma."
Some say that the term "dharma" found in the Sūtras refers exclusively to the meaning of the Vedas.

And it should not be argued: "In this view, although the study of the Veda is a cause for the investigation of the meaning of the Veda, it is not likewise a cause for the investigation of the meaning of the Smṛtis and so forth;

similarly, the study of a single recensional branch (*śākhā*)—which is what is denoted by the term *svādhyāya*—cannot possibly be a cause for the investigation of the meaning of other branches. Therefore, how can study be the cause for the investigation of the meaning of the entire Veda?

For [the answer is that] just as the injunction for study implies the necessity of investigation, so too does the determination of the meaning of the injunction for the performance of rituals according to a single branch [imply the need for broader inquiry].

Since it is accepted that the inquiry [into the Mīmāṃsā] has as its ultimate fruit the induction of an investigation into those [Vedic texts], because it depends upon the deliberation of sentences that convey the status of being subsidiary members (*aṅga*) according to other recensions (*śākhā*), its causality is established.

For this very reason, even for those who perform the practice of subsidiary elements obtained through Smṛti and custom (*ācāra*)—just like those obtained through direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*)—the investigation of the Smṛtis and so forth is also enjoined by the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) in order to determine the knowledge of the meaning of the performance injunctions (*prayogavidhi*). Therefore, it is indeed appropriate that this [Smṛti-investigation] also falls within the scope of the formal proposition (*pratijñā*).
Therefore, it is indeed appropriate that this [Self] is the subject of inquiry as the meaning of the Veda. Thus.
(An analysis of the category of *dharma* according to our own school's tenets:

In reality, since the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedas would be purposeless if it were not useful for engaging in or desisting from action, and because we do not observe prudent people in the world— who desire the attainment of happiness and the cessation of suffering— failing to practice the *dharma* and *adharma* that produce those results.
It is logical that, in reality, the investigation of that [Brahman] alone is taught as what ought to be performed;

for this very reason, the investigation of Dharma, which is obtained through the conduct of the Smṛtis and will be undertaken later, is not irrelevant. Nor can it be argued that because the word *atha* expresses the immediate succession to the study of the Veda, that [investigation of Dharma] alone is the primary meaning.
But the claim that [the word *atha*] is used by way of a contextual connection (*prasaṅga*) is correct;

for even though the word *atha* requires something previously mentioned, it is also appropriate as referring to the study of the Smṛtis, since there is no evidence that it signifies immediate succession to the study of the Vedas.
For this very reason, the Sūtra proposes only "the desire to know Dharma" (*dharmajijñāsā*).
And although the study of the entire Veda is not the cause for the investigation of dharma and adharma—
since the study of the Upaniṣads lacks that causal status—
nevertheless, it is indeed appropriate as a sequence [of study] even insofar as it is a cause for a single portion of the intended investigation; thus, there is no contradiction.
(The term *dharma* in *dharmajijñāsā* is indicative of *adharma*, etc.

Although it is stated there [in the *Jaiminisūtra*] simply as "the desire to know *dharma*," nevertheless, because the study of the Veda— which expounds *dharma*— would otherwise result in fruitlessness in the absence of an inquiry into *dharma*, [the term *dharma* is used in this extended sense].

Because it is the cause for the investigation of *dharma*, when the term *dharma* is used as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the study of prohibitions contained within the entirety of the Vedas, it should be understood as an indicator for *adharma* and so forth as well. Otherwise, if only *dharma* were the object of investigation, then since the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and other elements situated near injunctions could serve the purpose of investigating *dharma* by forming a single syntactical unit with those injunctions, the study of them would have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), just like [the study of] prohibitions and permissions in the absence of [an explicit mention of] *adharma*.

For that would result in the study of that [text] having only an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose. As for the purpose of using the word "dharma" as a general term—just as it serves as a synecdoche—it is simply to make known the necessity of investigating dharma by way of a concise summary of its many subjects. It is indeed logical that even when the subject of a rule of permission (abhyanujñā-vidhi) is being investigated for the sake of demonstrating certain exceptions to dharma and adharma, it is not irrelevant.
Therefore, with the intention that the *jijñāsā-sūtra* constitutes the formal proposition (*pratijñā*),

that the determination of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) alone constitutes the subject matter of the first chapter, and that the twelve subsequent chapters serve as its ancillary support (*parikara*), there is an investigation into the authority of Dharma regarding the prohibitions and explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) such as "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*) within the first chapter.
Furthermore, the investigation of dharma and adharma regarding the meaning of such sentences as "One should not eat *kalañja*" at the beginning of the sixth chapter is also not irrelevant;
with this very intention, it was stated by the venerable [Vidvan] Bhaṭṭarahasya that Jaimini investigated dharma and adharma within that twelve-chapter work (*dvādaśalakṣaṇī*).

Regarding the point that— in order to establish that the inquiry into *adharma* is the subject of the promise made in the opening sūtra (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*)— the *Śāstradīpikā* employs the elision of the vowel *a* (*akārapraśleṣa*) in the phrase "inquiry into *adharma*" (*adharmajijñāsā*) during its commentary on this sūtra:
that is improper, as it would entail the fault of repeating the sentence (*vākyāvṛttidoṣa*).

Furthermore, compared to the fault of sentence repetition, the acceptance of indication (lakṣaṇā) residing in the word has been asserted by everyone even in the case of the injunction for establishing the sacred fires, such as "one who has a son with black hair."

Or rather, since the repetition of the sentence in the Sūtra is not a defect because it functions as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), Adharma may also be the subject matter [of the inquiry] through the conjunction (*praśleṣa*) with the negative particle *a-* [in the word *adharma*]. (This concludes the refutation of the view of the author of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra*, who held that although Adharma must sometimes be defined as a rival to Dharma, only Dharma is the subject matter of the Śāstra.
As for what was stated by the author of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra*: "Even though Adharma is to be described in some instances as a rival to Dharma, only Dharma is the subject matter of the Śāstra."

Just as the investigation into the authority of the *arthavāda* passages such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest" (vāyurvai kṣepiṣṭha), which are recited in proximity to injunctions (*vidhi*), has been conducted by the Commentator and others, so too has the investigation into the authority regarding non-dharma (*adharma*) for those passages such as "He wept" (so 'rodīt) recited in proximity to prohibitions (*niṣedha*).
Therefore, it is improper [to claim] that [the two cases] are rivals, as their rivalry is difficult to maintain.

For just as the state of being an opponent to difference is not possible in non-difference because it consists in the absence of difference, so too it is not appropriate for unrighteousness (*adharma*) to consist in the absence of righteousness (*dharma*),
since in that case, acts such as eating would result in being unrighteous due to the absence of the nature of righteousness.

Therefore, it is correct that while dharma and adharma were introduced with equal status in the first sūtra, they are subsequently investigated in this treatise along with their definitions, means of knowledge, results, and fallacious counterparts.
(An investigation into dharma as sacrifice and the like:
Although, in the Kaṇāda school, the terms *dharma* and *adharma* denote the *apūrva* (unseen potency),
this is because such usage is observed even in passages such as "Dharma perishes through [failure of] recitation."

And thus, although it is not appropriate for the apūrva (the unseen potency) to be the subject of the treatise’s formal proposition— since there is no inquiry into the apūrva in each individual chapter— nevertheless, because the term ‘dharma’ is applied even by those devoid of knowledge of the apūrva when they perform acts such as sacrifice, and because of the Vedic injunction ‘Practice dharma,’ as well as in the words of the Blessed One and others such as: “But dharma is that which consists of the stories of Viṣvaksena when practiced by men,” [it is established].

"If one does not produce delight [in yoga], it is indeed nothing but weariness," and so forth; and in the Smṛti: "Of the acts of sacrifice, conduct, compassion, non-violence, charity, and Vedic study—this, however, is the supreme dharma: the perception of the Self through Yoga"; and in the passage, "Among these, O Brāhmaṇa, this is the supreme [dharma]," there is the cognition that sacrifice and the other acts possess the nature of *dharma*, just as the quality of being a Brāhmaṇa is cognized in that which is designated by the word ending in the genitive case. This is with respect to the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).

Since the application [of the term] is possible even through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by way of the relation of being produced from entities consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—which are respectively enjoined and prohibited—the words *dharma* and *adharma* do not denote the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

Rather, they are primarily potent (*śakta*) only with respect to the actions, qualities, substances, and so forth that produce them; thus, it is precisely action and the like, in their own form, that constitute the subject of the formal proposition (*pratijñā*) of this inquiry.
This is entirely correct.

Since the distinction of its own nature is established by the first two chapters, and the means for that [realization] and so forth are investigated by the third chapter onwards, the entire treatise constitutes the preliminary equipment for the desire to know (jijñāsā).

Since it is impossible to define the essential nature of dharma and adharma without first establishing the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) through its definition, the second sūtra— *codanālakṣaṇo ’rtho dharmaḥ* (Jaimini 1.1.2)— is intended to make known the nature of the means of valid cognition by means of excluding both non-connection with and connection to other things.
(Since the term *codanā* refers to the Veda, even that which is enjoined by injunctions inferred from mantras and the like obtains the status of *dharma*.

That which is sought—that is, desired—by virtue of being a producer of a result, is *dharma* as defined by the authority of *codanā*; that is to say, it is that which has the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) as its authority, namely *codanā*.

In this regard, since the *jijñāsā-sūtra* (1.1.1) proposes the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for dharma in general, and since the Smṛti text "The entire Veda is the root of dharma" and others establish that the Veda alone is its authority; and since in the *codanā-sūtra* (1.1.2) as well, the term *codanā*—by virtue of being the locus where the capacity to impel action is fully realized—denotes injunctive sentences including mantras, arthavādas, and names, and thus has the entire Veda as its scope; and since arthavādas and the like will subsequently be determined to be authorities for dharma and adharma; and since the study of the Veda is construed as the antecedent to the [inquiry]—the sūtra is indeed intent upon the Veda.

Therefore, it is stated in the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*: "Thus, the acceptance of the means of valid cognition as indicated by the *codanā*, along with its various modes, has been elaborated upon by the first definition. This is likewise seen in the *Vārttika*: "Now, the utility of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras is being discussed in every respect regarding the Veda, whose status as a means of valid cognition is already established, with respect to *dharma*."

They maintain that even under the restrictive rule that "only injunctive statements (*codanā*) are authoritative," the subsequent determination of the authority of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is not inconsistent;
according to their view, the inclusion of the Veda alone as the authority for defining dharma and adharma remains perfectly secure.
Therefore, since those things enjoined by injunctions inferred from mantras, explanatory passages, and so forth, are based on the Veda as their authority, they attain the status of dharma.
(An exposition of the view of Pārthasārathi Miśra: that *codanā* refers to a collection of words that makes known the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)):

However, according to the opinion of those for whom—although in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra* only the source of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding dharma and adharma was proposed—in the *Codanā-sūtra*, the word "codanā" is used here as a well-known synonym for "upadeśa" and "vidhi," [stating] "codanā, upadeśa, and vidhi denote one and the same thing. Thus, its status as a source of knowledge is established.

Based on the natural sense of numerous passages in the Bhāṣya and Vārtika beginning with "dharme prati codanāyāḥ," and by virtue of the etymological derivation of its parts, [the term *codanā*] refers exclusively to a collection of words (*vākya*) that conveys an action qualified by the "thing-to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*) and so forth—which is another name for the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*).
Furthermore, the restrictive rule is that this alone is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

This is because, if [the term] were taken to denote injunctive sentences accompanied by mantras, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and names—serving as the locus where the capacity to incite action is fully present—then even if the definition might somehow apply to the initial investigation of *arthavādas*, the investigation of *smṛtis* and other sources excluded from that category would result in being irrelevant.

Nor does your own position suffer from a violation of the restrictive rule that "the Vedic injunction alone [is the means of valid knowledge]," by virtue of defining other means of valid knowledge (pramāṇas) besides the injunction;

for it is well known that restrictive rules have as their result the exclusion of those things belonging to the same class [as the thing being restricted]. Furthermore, since explanatory passages (arthavādas), traditional texts (smṛtis), and so forth, are subordinate to the injunction and are rooted in it, they do not possess the status of a means of valid knowledge equal to the injunction.

For this very reason, the validity of explanatory passages, traditional texts, and the like—which occupy the place of the "procedure" (itikartavyatā)—is established by the very same proposition that establishes the validity of the injunction.

Because the first characteristic was promised in its entirety, the Teacher stated that it serves as a supplement to the *Codanā-sūtra* in the passage beginning with "That which is indicated by the *Codanā-sūtra*," and so forth.

And since that [characteristic] is praiseworthy, when the means of valid knowledge regarding Dharma— consisting of the form "one should accomplish heaven and so forth by means of this rite assisted by this mantra"—
is being produced by the *codanā*, [the name-words function] by way of reminding one of the word-meanings and by way of determining the specific instrument.

From the inclusion of the word "parigraha" (acceptance), it is understood that memory and the other factors, which serve as auxiliary causes, fall within the scope of the proposition regarding the authority of the *codanā* by virtue of being its presenters;
however, this much alone does not constitute a demonstration of the authority of the *codanā*, for that would be untenable.

However, if that [definition] were accepted merely as a possibility for everything in this chapter, then because that very [definition] is employed from the beginning through to the conclusion, it would be logically consistent. Therefore, in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*,

having accepted the word *codanā* as denoting merely the collection of words that enjoin activity toward the object of the three-fold cultivation (*bhāvanā*)— as much as has been introduced regarding the entire body of means of knowledge for dharma and adharma— the status of being the primary authority for dharma and adharma belongs to that alone.

That which was proposed in the *Codanāsūtra* has been examined in its entirety in the first pāda. This was done for the sake of strengthening the acceptance [of the Vedas] by establishing the equality— due to their being non-human (apauruṣeya)— between the Vedic portions such as the *arthavādas* that exceed the *codanās*, and the Smṛtis and other such texts that are subordinate.

Because it has been introduced, the validity (prāmāṇya) that was desired to be known and promised in the first sūtra is now being examined as a relevant digression; thus, the view intended by Pārthasārathi Miśra is indeed correct.

(Establishing the previously stated view by refuting the views of others: In their opinion, *codanā*—which is synonymous with the statement of an injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*)—is that which constitutes its definition.

For this very reason, those who argue for the means [of valid knowledge] formulate its definition as "being that which has the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), which is the object intended by the injunction," and so forth.

Nevertheless, since the term "Vedic" (*vaidika*) must necessarily be included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to those things that are the objects of worldly injunctions (*laukikacodanā*) yet possess the status of being means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), it is more appropriate—on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*)—to employ only the word "Veda" (*veda*) while abandoning the word "injunction" (*vidhi*).

Alternatively, even if one were to argue that there is no status as an injunction (*vidhitva*) in the case of the use of worldly optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth because they do not provide knowledge of what was previously unknown (*ajñātajñāpakatva*), and thus that exclusion is achieved by the word "injunction" alone; [the use of "Veda" remains necessary for the reasons stated above].

Nevertheless, since it is the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) themselves that serve as the authority regarding the cognition of being a means to achieve a desired end—which is rooted in both mantras and *arthavādas*—the venerable author of the *Bhāṭṭarahasya*, intending to ensure that this [definition] applies universally, has stated a definition incorporating the Veda itself: "Dharma-ness consists in having the status of a means to the highest good (*śreyas*) as cognized by the Veda; Adharma-ness consists in having the status of a means to the undesirable (*aniṣṭa*) as cognized by the Veda."
(An application of the definition of *dharma* as stated in the *Bhāṭṭarahasya*, preceded by an examination of its purpose, to the objects of that definition:
This [definition] applies to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the eating of *kalañja*, and so forth;
for in both cases, their status as means to the desirable and the undesirable is taught by the Veda.
The latter part [of the definition]—that "it is made known by the Veda"—applies even to Brahman, heaven, hell, and so forth;
for these, being of the nature of the desired or the undesired, do not themselves possess the status of being means [to those ends].

The first part [of the definition] is included to exclude cases such as eating food or poison, where there is indeed the attainment of the desired (satisfaction) or the undesired (death), yet they are not the means [to those ends] in the required sense.
Because the fact that these [means] are instruments for achieving that [end] is understood from worldly experience itself;
and "being taught by the Veda" consists in being the object of a sublating cognition in the form of a knowledge of the unknown produced by the Veda.

Therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the knowledge of the Self—which is the means for removing ignorance (denoted by the word *śoka*) as expressed in such sentences as "Fire is the remedy for cold," or "The knower of the Self transcends sorrow"—nor to fire, which produces the removal of cold.
Because the fact that it is a means to that [result] is known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It is precisely for the sake of attaining such a state of "making known what was previously unknown" that [the author] has explained it in that very same place as "being made known by the Veda while not being independently made known by any means of valid cognition other than the Veda," and so forth.
For this very reason, "unknownness" (*ajñātatva*) should also be understood as being produced by another means of knowledge that does not depend upon itself.

Therefore, there is no non-pervasion (avyāpti) regarding those things whose status as a means to a desired end is understood through Smṛti and other sources rooted in direct perception and Śruti; for even the state of being a means to a desired or undesired end that is apprehended at first glance is indeed taught by the Veda. To exclude over-pervasion (ativyāpti) in such cases, the term "unsublated" (abādhita) is included. Furthermore, the word "Veda" does not refer here to the entire collection of Mantra and Brāhmaṇa texts as it does in the injunction for the recitation of the Vedas (pārāyaṇa-vidhi).
Because that would lead to the consequence of impossibility;
nor does it intend the meaning of the sentences contained therein,
because that [consequence] would not apply to what is established by a sentence whose indicative power (*liṅga*) and so forth are inferred.
Rather, it refers to non-human (apauruṣeya) speech.

Nor should it be argued that there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of *apūrva* to Brahman, because he too is the cause of the world, is a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ*), and that [status] is knowable solely through the Veda, such as the passage beginning "from which..."— for in the definition,
what is intended is the possession of causality as determined by an effectness delimited by that specific excellence of the highest good (*tacchreyastvāvacchinnakāryatānirūpitakāraṇatā*).
Furthermore, the state of excellence (*śreyas*) here is that which has its own well-known supreme fruit;

therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the subsidiaries such as the *prayāja* offerings by taking their fruit to be the removal of defects in the sacrifice, nor to substances, deities, and so forth by taking their fruit to be the performance of the oblation and other acts. Even though the prohibition contained within the context of the sacrifice, "one shall not speak untruth," does not convey the production of undesirable results in the form of hell, the status of unrighteousness (*adharma*) is established for speaking untruth and the like simply by conveying the production of a deficiency in the sacrifice.
Thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in that case;
furthermore, the conventional usage of the absence of the nature of *dharma* (*dharmatva*) regarding the auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) is found in the Bhāṣya: "What is *dharma*?
What are the means (*sādhana*)?"
Thus, for one who desires to know the essential nature [of dharma], it is clearly understood through the desire to know its distinct means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

For those who know the performance of the *vājapeya* sacrifice, the conventional usage "this person is righteous" (*dhārmika*) with respect to its performer is based on a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the property of being a constituent part of the *vājapeya*—which is the primary factor—to the means of accomplishment.

However, for those who do not know the performance of the *vājapeya*, the usage of that term with respect to a performer of only one part of it is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), based on the similarity to the state of performing an enjoined action.
Since it is frequently observed in common worldly usage that a word employed for a whole is also applied to its parts;

and since the injunction regarding false speech for the sake of marriage teaches merely the non-production of the fault that causes the transgression of a prohibition— not the production of something desirable— there is no over-extension [of the definition] there, as it lacks the defining characteristic of dharma.

Furthermore, because the prohibition "one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra*" does not imply that it is a means to an undesirable result— since this would contradict the injunction for its taking—

and because even in its absence the benefit to the sacrifice is accomplished by other constituent parts, the *ṣoḍaśin* cup-offering does not constitute unrighteousness (*adharma*) despite being subject to prohibition.

(Justification for the nature of self-knowledge as Dharma): Alternatively, because the term "dharma" is applied even to the knowledge of the Self in such passages as: "But this is the supreme dharma: the vision of the Self through yoga, [accompanied] by the practices of right conduct, compassion, non-violence, charity, and the study of sacred texts."

Since it is not known through any means of valid cognition that the vision of the Self— accompanied by hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption— is the generator of the cessation of beginningless, indefinable ignorance in the form of a positive entity, and since it is stated that the knowledge of the Self produced by yoga is the supreme dharma specifically in its qualified aspect,
it is logical that even in the case of knowledge, it is indeed a dharma.

Nor should it be argued: "Even if Upaniṣadic passages such as 'The knower of the Self overcomes grief' are of the nature of *arthavāda* (laudatory statements), the injunction to know the Self—such as 'One should effect the knowledge of the Self'—is perceived through their originative force (*utpatti-pratīti*), since that [injunction] must be postulated from them.

For even if such sentences are of the nature of *arthavāda*, the perception of the originative force of the injunction to know the Self—namely, that one should effect the knowledge of the Self which is postulated from them—is uncontradicted.

When there is an inquiry into the fruit of the knowledge of the Self—which is the subject matter of that injunction—the cessation of beginningless ignorance, which is synonymous with "sorrow," is perceived as the fruit from the explanatory passage (arthavāda), "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow. Since this perception is itself uncontradicted, the status of [Self-knowledge] as a duty (dharma) is established through the possibility of its being characterized [as such]. Furthermore, within the context of the section concerning the injunctions for hearing [the Vedas] and so forth, there exists the clear injunction, "The Self, indeed, is to be seen"; thus, there is no need for the laborious effort of postulating such an injunction.
Nor is there an impossibility of injunction regarding knowledge on the grounds that it is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object;

for even though knowledge is not itself directly enjoined, its status as an object of injunction is established by its being occupied with activities such as the application of the mind (*manas*) favorable to it—just as time, space, and so forth are occupied by their respective substrates.
Otherwise, since hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other such acts ultimately consist of the nature of knowledge, injunctions such as "one should hear" would likewise be impossible in their case as well.

By this [it is shown that]: since an injunction is untenable with respect to knowledge, one must accept that the suffix *tavya* in the word "to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) has the sense of fitness (*arha*). Consequently, because it is neither enjoined nor prohibited, the knowledge of the Self is entirely outside the sphere of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
For this very reason, the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*) is distinct from the two sections concerning ritual action (*karman*) and meditation (*upāsanā*).
In the passage "But this is the supreme duty," the word "vision" (*darśana*) ends in the instrumental *lyuṭ* suffix.

And thus, since it is the *nirvikalpa-samādhi* (non-conceptual absorption) alone—which serves as the means for self-knowledge through yoga ending with *savikalpa-samādhi* (conceptual absorption)—that is expressed by the term "vision of the Self" (*ātmadarśana*), it is that [absorption] which possesses the nature of *dharma*, not self-knowledge itself. As for the statement made by some—that if one does not accept the suffix *-lyuṭ* [in the word *darśana*], then because all fruits of action are included within the fruit of knowledge, the description of knowledge as the supreme goal is merely figurative praise; this is refuted.

Since it is improper to assume that the texts have a meaning that is largely useless when it is possible for them to be intended as instruction directed toward imparting self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) to those people who— having their internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) permeated by beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*) and submerged in *saṃsāra*— have not even heard a report of self-knowledge; and because, although meditations (*upāsanā*) are indeed *dharma*, a distinction from the *Karmakāṇḍa* is established by taking some specific form as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the object of inquiry, so too, although knowledge is *dharma*, its distinction from both the *Karma* and *Upāsanā* sections is logically justified.

Furthermore, there is no reason to abandon the sense of the word *darśana* as naturally understood—namely, that its fruit is the knowledge of the Self possessed by the wise—and instead to assume it refers to a means (*sādhana*) by interpreting the suffix *-lyuṭ* as an instrument;

for the term "yoga" denotes the entire system culminating in non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), and there is no authoritative basis for restricting it to only one part thereof.

Indeed, if it were not intended to convey the knowledge of the meaning manifested through laughter and so forth, the sentence "This is the supreme Brāhmaṇa among these" would not be applied to a non-Brāhmaṇa such as a Śūdra.
Because there is no intention (*tātparya*) in the primary words to convey a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*),

on the contrary— just as by the phrase "the supreme Brāhmaṇa" one understands the Brāhmaṇahood of others indicated by the genitive case, so too in this sentence, by the statement that knowledge is dharma, one understands that sacrifice (*ijyā*) and the rest are indeed dharma.
Furthermore, since the Bhaṭṭālaṅkāras have established that sacrificial acts and the like possess the nature of dharma,
it is therefore entirely logical that the knowledge of the Self is also dharma.

(Also, even obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites possess the nature of *dharma* by virtue of being means for the destruction of sin; therein follows the justification of the view of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*.
Nor [should it be argued]: "Since no fruit is heard of in the injunctions for obligatory and occasional rites, how can these fall within the scope of the previously stated definition of *dharma*?"

This must be said: even in that case, according to the method established by Miśra and others in the *Sarvāśakti-adhikaraṇa*, since there is a necessary assumption of a result consisting in the destruction of sin—based on Smṛti texts such as "Standing while reciting the morning prayer (*sandhyā*), one casts off the sin of the night," and Mantras such as "Whatever sin I have committed by night"—the status of these acts as *dharma* is established because they possess the previously mentioned definition.
Although this is not the view of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, [it remains valid].

As was stated by him in the *Yāvajjīvādhikaraṇa*: "If all sins were destroyed merely by the performance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*), what intelligent person would engage in the performance of the *agnihotra* and other rites? But if it is the destruction of only one [sin], it cannot be determined which [sin] that is."

Nevertheless, according to that [view], since it is accepted that the non-performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth performed at their proper time results in the absence of the fault produced by such non-performance, or that performing them at another time produces demerit (*pāpa*), and that the destruction of that [demerit] is the result; and since it is accepted from the aforementioned Smṛti texts and mantras that these must be performed even when the [original] time has passed for the sake of destroying the fault arising from the non-performance of what was prescribed— therefore, [the performance of rites at a later time] is indeed possible according to that view.
Even for them, the nature of phenomena (dharmatva) is as previously described.
(An establishment that just as substances such as curd possess the nature of dharma, so too substances such as silver possess the nature of adharma:

And thus, just as in the case of substances, qualities, times, and so forth— such as "curd for one desiring sensory power," "if Parjanya is to rain, one should measure the Sadas shed low," and "in the sixth [month] for one desiring food"— which have been enjoined by injunctions as the means to various respective excellences (*śreyas*);
Because it possesses the characteristics previously stated, it is *dharma*;

likewise, it is also logical that substances such as silver, which are indicated by prohibitions like "silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)", possess the nature of *adharma* due to their being means to undesirable results.

Furthermore, it is the statement of a certain deluded person that is correct here: by the prohibitive sentence, one understands merely that [the giving of silver] is not a means for accomplishing [the sacrifice], but not that it is a means for achieving something undesirable; for if that were the case, then even if the giver of silver were to accept the undesirable [consequence], it would not result in a deficiency of the ritual (*ṛtuvaiguṇya*).

For when silver is directly perceived as the means for giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) upon the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), it is impossible—even by hundreds of injunctions—to produce a cognition that it is not a means for that purpose, just as one cannot produce a cognition of non-identity with the sacrificer.
Indeed, in this case, unlike the prohibition of things for the sake of human ends, the status of being a means to hell is not implied merely to avoid the futility of the prohibition;
otherwise, the employment of the word "barhis" (sacrificial grass) would result in being redundant.

However, just like the prohibition "one should not speak untruth" within the context of a ritual (*ṛtu*), this [prohibition against giving] merely causes a deficiency in the ritual; if that were understood as applying to the act of giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in general, then it would follow that even the giving of gold and other such items would cause a deficiency in the ritual.

And so, just as it is established by injunction that "one gives a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's faith," when a gift related to the sacrifice is prescribed, the very fact that silver serves as its material is what is inferred to cause a deficiency in the rite— just as the fact that curd serves as the material for a *homa* produces the fruit of sensory power (*indriya*). Since this much alone is universally accepted as the basis for the status of "dharma" in the case of curd and other such substances, let them consider what specific distinction there could be such that they do not likewise declare silver and other such materials to be "adharma."

Therefore, with this very intention, the venerable [author] stated in the *Bhaṭṭarahasya*: "For there is no distinction in worldly usage such as 'this person is righteous' or 'that person is unrighteous' among those who perform subsidiary rites for the sake of a fruit, nor among those who employ silver and the like in a sacrifice.

For this very reason, the lack of excellence (*aprāśastya*) regarding silver—which is understood from prohibitions to be a means to an undesirable result—is made known by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*).

And in the absence of such an indicator, since it is specifically the qualified action that is prohibited, its status as a producer of an undesirable result is established, just as in the case of eating forbidden food (kalañja) and so forth; thus it has been stated.
(Refutation of the over-extension of the definition of demerit to the latent impressions of non-dual ignorance, etc.

Although the definition of demerit—as that which possesses the quality of being a means to the undesirable, as taught in Upanishadic passages such as, "Sunless indeed are those worlds, enveloped in blind darkness;
to them they go after death, those people who are slayers of the Self"—is over-extended (*ativyāpta*) to the latent impressions of non-dual ignorance (*avidyādvaitavāsanā*) and the like;

Nevertheless, since this [passage] is primarily intent upon praising the knowledge of the Self-knowing one—and thus, by means of *lakṣaṇā* (implied meaning), is intent upon extolling the excellence of self-knowledge—the cognition of the literal sense as it appears on the surface is sublated by the subsequent *lakṣaṇā*. Consequently, because there is an absence of the status of being a means to an undesirable end with respect to that which is the object of an unsublated cognition, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). However, if it were to be assumed that an injunction exists—namely, "one should abandon the latent impression of duality through such censure"—for the purpose of avoiding that fault, [the problem would remain].
Since renunciation is enjoined in that context, it is indeed dharma; thus, there is no inconsistency.

Therefore, it is entirely logical that the definition of dharma is "that which has the quality of being a means to the highest good as taught by the Veda," and the definition of adharma is "that which has the quality of being a means to the undesirable as taught by that [Veda]"; such is the pair of definitions.

(Refinement of the Definition of Dharma: Being Revealed by the Veda) Here, this should be noted: if "being revealed by the Veda" means being the object of a non-sublated cognition produced by the Veda, and if that [cognition] is taken as being of the nature of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*),...

In that case, although in the instance of an injunction (*vidhi*)— due to the co-occurrence with words such as "heaven" (*svarga*)— the relationship of means and end between the sacrifice and heaven is indeed the object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*),

in your own view, in the case of a prohibition (*niṣedha*), since the status of being a means to an undesirable result (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*) is admitted to be understood through mere implication (*ākṣepa*) due to the absence of co-occurrence with a word denoting the undesirable, how can the status of being a means to an undesirable result residing in the prohibited act be the object of the cognition consisting of a verbal cognition produced by the Veda?

If [the definition] were "being the object of a cognition produced by the Veda," then how could that apply even to Brahman, heaven, hell, and so forth? Since this was stated [by the author], the formulation of the second part of the definition becomes consistent with what was said by the venerable teacher in the *Bhaṭṭarahasya*.

Therefore, because the definition of Dharma is uniform, it is proper to formulate the definition of Adharma as well as: "the state of being a means to an undesirable result, which is the object of an inference produced by the Veda."

Even regarding the knowledge of the Self, if there is an injunction such as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, it is to be heard," then there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti), because the status of being a means to a desired end— namely, the cessation of ignorance which is the object of the inferential cognition prompted by that injunction— is not absent. However, when that [injunction] does not possess the nature of an injunction, [then the definition applies].
In that case, let there be no status as *dharma* for the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*).

However, regarding the statement "this is the supreme *dharma*," one can also say that what is intended to be expressed as *dharma* is the nature of action (*kriyārūpa*), such as sacrifice (*yajña*), and not the knowledge of the Self; thus, there is no fault.
(The position that the Śyena sacrifice possesses the nature of dharma:
Since both types of characteristics are present in the Śyena, it indeed possesses the nature of dharma;
however, its non-dharma nature belongs specifically to the *abhicāra* (malevolent rite) consisting of violence, which is the fruit of the Śyena—this will be clarified in the fourth [book].

(The demonstration that [the Śyena sacrifice] is not non-dharma because it is not something to be prohibited, and that it is indeed non-dharma because it is connected with a powerful undesirable consequence.

As for the objection raised by the author of the *Bhaṭṭālaṅkāra*: "If one includes 'not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence' within the definition of dharma, then since the Śyena is enjoined, how could it be connected with a powerful undesirable consequence when it is not the object of the prohibition 'one must not kill'?"—having raised this doubt:
This is because the resolve, "I must cause the death of my enemy,"—though prompted by passion—is subject to prohibition as it is touched by the destruction of the injunction;

or else, because the performer of the *śyena* sacrifice incurs a transgression of the prohibition regarding the act conducive to the enemy's death (the fruit of the *śyena*), which can be accomplished through visible means [such as poison], that [prohibition] is thus justified. Furthermore, it has been stated that this [act] does not incur the status of being denotable by the term "unrighteousness" (*adharma*), because even though it is followed by undesirable consequences, it lacks the quality of being prohibited in its own essential nature.

Since that which is prohibited is itself unrighteousness (*adharma*), if the term "unrighteousness" is used in common worldly usage for something that is not itself prohibited but is connected to undesirable consequences through a causal chain, then let the *śyena* sacrifice and the like be considered unrighteousness— thus it has been stated.

(An exposition on the prohibition of *abhicāra* [malevolent magic] and a refutation of the position that the *śyena* sacrifice is unrighteous): In this context, it has been stated that the resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—"I must bring about the death of my enemy"—is untouched by any injunction (*vidhi*). This is because the resolve necessarily precedes the performance of the *śyena*; and if the ritual act were enjoined, then its preceding resolve would also have to be enjoined either by the scriptural text enjoining the act itself or by some other scriptural authority.

Alternatively, even in the absence of being something to be performed (*vidheya*), [the action] is unavoidable because it is invariably concomitant with the ritual act (*karma*); otherwise, even in the case of the injury to an animal in the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, the resolve "the killing of the animal must be done by me" would be subject to prohibition, which would entail its being connected with an undesirable result of great weight (*balavadaniṣṭānubandhitva*). Furthermore, since the resolve is the object of prohibition, the possibility of its being connected with an undesirable result of great weight would apply even to the *śyena* sacrifice, which is itself enjoined.

Furthermore, even though the Śyena sacrifice is a subject of prohibition when its means are perceived, it is impossible to speak of a transgression of the prohibition regarding that which has been enjoined.

Since there is no absence of unrighteousness (*adharma*) due to the absence of being prohibited by its very nature, and since there is no obstacle to accepting its status as righteousness (*dharma*) by virtue of being enjoined by its very nature, there is no purpose in including "not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence" [as a definition of dharma].
Nor should it be argued that it must indeed be unrighteous because it is connected with an undesirable consequence through a mediated sequence; for...

Just as there is the utilization of bronze vessels for the purpose of seeking knowledge (*vividiṣā*) and so forth through the renunciation of desire, so too, in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice, if its aspect of producing the fruit of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) were renounced and it were utilized for the purpose of seeking knowledge and so forth, it would possess the nature of dharma.

However, since the *śyena* and similar rites are in no way free from being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānubandhitva*), there is no cause whatsoever for engagement; thus, engagement with them is logically untenable.

Therefore, it must be stated that the *śyena* sacrifice is indeed a dharma, but is considered *adharma* only because it is indirectly connected to undesirable consequences (*aniṣṭa*). Consequently, since it is incorrect to designate it as *adharma* on the grounds of its indirect connection to undesirable results, and since there is no purpose for including "not being followed by powerful undesirable consequences" in the definition of dharma, it is logical that the status of dharma belongs to the *śyena* and similar acts themselves, while the status of *adharma* belongs only to the *abhicāra* (malevolent magic) consisting of violence, which is the fruit of the *śyena*.
And this very point has been established in the *Śāstradīpikā* under the *Codanāsūtra*.
(An explanation of the non-dharmic nature of the Śyena sacrifice according to another scriptural statement:

How, then, are the following both possible: the prescription of expiation, "Having performed the officiating for Vrātyas, the funeral rites for others, malevolent magic (abhicāra), and the Ahīna sacrifice, one is purified by three Kṛcchra penances," as well as the censure of the learned?

This is because, by considering such statements as "That which is for the purpose of destroying another is declared to be tāmasa," and through the force of the prohibition inferred from the censure of its tāmasa nature, one understands that it is a direct cause of hell; thus, since it possesses the quality of unrighteousness (adharma), its [classification as such] is justified.

(The absence of the scope of the *nahinindā* maxim in the case of the censure of the hawk). Nor should it be argued that— just as in the case of the conflict with the direct injunctions regarding the *udita* and *anudita* times for the fire-oblation (*homa*), it is impossible to assume prohibitions inferred from the censures even when they are recited in proximity— because in that instance, although the contradiction can be resolved by the *nahinindā* maxim through the purpose of praising the enjoined act, in the present case...

Because the discussion concerns the instruction on the threefold nature of action, and because censure would otherwise be rendered meaningless in the absence of mutual praise—thereby necessitating the assumption of prohibitions; and likewise, since sacrifices and other rites are also established as being threefold according to the distinction of the qualities such as *sattva*, the Commentator has stated [in the introduction to the verse beginning with] "But there is a remedy for all this" (*parihārastvapi sarvasya*) that he intends to show how one might indeed abandon them through the perception of their being *rājasa* and *tāmasa*, and instead perform only those that are *sāttvika*. Furthermore, this is because he has approved of the assumption of both prohibitions and injunctions in that introductory passage.
Furthermore, according to the maxim that "the relative strength and weakness of those [scriptural texts] obstructed by meaninglessness is reversed," even the Smṛti rule possesses greater authority.

Moreover, if one were to postulate a prohibition based on a deprecatory statement, then since such Tāmasa action would also be something enjoined, it would follow that it must always be performed by the learned (śiṣṭas).
Otherwise, even Tāmasa sacrifices and the like would not fall within the scope of prohibition.

This is because, just as there is a threefold classification of enjoined action, one must—whether unwillingly or not—admit that the statement regarding its being *tāmasa* refers specifically to acts such as the *śyena* sacrifice; for it is impossible to say that [the definition] does not apply to the *śyena* and similar acts.

Nor is it the case that this statement of the Blessed One, because of its threefold nature, is intended solely to describe the threefold classification [of sacrifices], since it is observed from the preceding context that other reasons for the *tāmasa* nature of *pākayajña* and other rites are stated in such passages as: "They declare a sacrifice devoid of injunction, lacking offered food, devoid of mantras, without sacrificial fees, and bereft of faith to be *tāmasa*. How, then, can that statement have the *śyena* and other such sacrifices as its subject?
Is this reasonable?

It must be said: even if the Lord’s intent is merely to teach the threefold sequence of practices such as those characterized by *sattva* and so forth, there is no intent to define their characteristics as mutually exclusive; otherwise, recitation (*japa*), austerity (*tapas*), charity (*dāna*), and burnt offerings (*homa*) performed without mantras and contrary to injunctions would result in being non-tāmasa.

Furthermore, there would be no occurrence of *tāmasatva* (the quality of darkness) in a sacrifice performed for the purpose of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) unless there were a cause for its *tāmasatva* inherent in the sacrifice itself;

for the cause of *tāmasatva* in austerity—namely, the infliction of pain upon others—is present in such sacrifices and gifts as well, and thus it would be difficult even for the Blessed One to establish the absence of *tāmasatva* in them.

Moreover, by explicit prohibitions such as "one should not practice even a dharma that leads to heaven if it is loathed by the world," [it is established that] a means of performing a dharma that results in nothing but an unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭa*) other than heaven [is condemned].
This is because [acts] such as sacrifice, giving, oblation, and austerity are understood to be means for attaining hell.

By this same reasoning, even in cases such as the Śyena sacrifice—which generates malevolent magic (*abhicāra*)—where there is an injunction specifically for a sacrifice of that nature, as in "one who desires the death of an enemy directly should sacrifice," the prohibition against killing does not apply because it is [itself] enjoined. Furthermore, [this applies to] dharma which, even through a mediated sequence, does not produce an undesirable result.
The unrighteousness of the sacrifice must be established.

Nor should it be argued: "In the statement 'for the purpose of destroying another,' since the word *utsādana* (destruction) ending in the instrumental *lyuṭ* suffix denotes an activity conducive to the destruction of another, it is understood that the *tāmasa* nature belongs only to the *śyena* sacrifice and similar rites which serve that purpose, and not to the sacrifice itself which is directly of the nature of *abhicāra* (malevolent magic); how then can it be an object of censure by virtue of being *tāmasa*?

This objection should not be raised, because when the *tāmasa* nature of the *śyena* and other such rites—which produce *abhicāra*—is stated, the *tāmasa* nature of the action that is directly of the form of *abhicāra* is established by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutikanyāya*).

Therefore, because they share an identical status in terms of security and risk (*tulyayogakṣematayā*), both of those which are censurable—the malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) and the action that produces it—are subsumed under the term "malevolent rite" (*abhicāra*) in the expression "the malevolent rite and what is inferior."

Nor is the term *abhicāra* here intended to refer to worldly sorcery; for, by its mention alongside prescribed sacrifices, gifts, *ahīna* rites, and *antyakarma*, it is understood as referring specifically to prescribed sorcery.
Or, let it be that the term refers to both types of sorcery.
Even by that much, there is no fault. Therefore,

since there is no obstacle to accepting merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) in the form of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as in the case of a single hawk and so forth during the Mahābhārata war, it is entirely reasonable— following the previously stated definition of *dharma* and *adharma*— to postulate a reduction in hell for the sake of making the scriptural injunction meaningful.
The nature of being dharma and the nature of being adharma [are established] in the case of the Śyena sacrifice and so forth; this is the general direction [of the argument].

(Refutation of the Invalidity of the Vedas) Once the nature of dharma and adharma has been established through the two previously mentioned definitions, their means of valid cognition is as follows: since of the two previously mentioned definitions, it is impossible for them not to be taught by the Veda, the Veda alone is the authority on this basis of the statement, "The entire Veda is the root of dharma."
Furthermore, because the Veda is inherently free from human authorship and thus devoid of defects, it is not impossible for it to generate a cognition of an uncontradicted object.
To generate a cognition of a contradicted object constitutes invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*),
and that [invalidity] is of two kinds.
Or [it is due to] the knowledge of a defect in the cause. Regarding the cognition produced by the Veda, there is certainly no direct falsity in that cognition itself;

for that [falsity] would have to arise either from a lack of informative capacity (*abodhakatva*), from having already been known (and thus being redundant), or from the object to be known not existing as it is represented.
In this regard, it cannot first of all be said that the Veda is non-cognitive,

because the cognition of the meaning of a sentence arising from Vedic words— which possess expectancy and the like and whose relations [to their meanings] have been grasped— is established by experience.
Nor can it be said that it cognizes what has already been cognized;

Since the absence of [the relationship between] sacrifice and the like being the means and heaven being the end from among the objects of perception and so forth was already refuted in the very *Sūtra* on perception (*pratyakṣa-sūtra*), the non-existence of such a state in cognition would have to be due to one of two reasons: either the absence of any proof establishing that it is an object of knowledge produced by qualities such as causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), or due to a subverting means of knowledge (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). Of these, the first is certainly not the case.
Because there is no purpose in considering qualities such as causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*) for a cognition that has arisen through correspondence with its object;

and because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in using such [correspondence] as a determinant of being non-erroneous, since even dream-objects that do not possess such [correspondence] are seen to produce causal efficacy.
Furthermore, the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is itself a cognition that [itself] knows "that is false."
Alternatively, [the Veda] would be characterized by being made known through defective instruments;
yet, the cognition that the meaning of the Veda is false is not possible,

because in the case of injunctions for results such as heaven, the objection that a momentary action cannot produce a result in the next world has been refuted by the acceptance of an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*).

Furthermore, regarding paintings and the like, although their objects are real, there is no contradiction because—according to the logic of the fourth [chapter]—their results may be perceived either in this life or in the next, and thus the non-perception of an immediate result does not constitute a sublation.

As for the fruit of the *kārīrī* sacrifice, even though its nature is to be experienced in this life, it is possible that it is not perceived immediately due to defects in the performance; therefore, in that case as well, there is no sublation.

(An establishment of the non-human authorship of the Vedas, preceded by a demonstration that the inference of their human authorship is fallacious due to its being subject to a *upādhi* such as "having a basis in another means of valid cognition"):
Furthermore, it is not possible for [the Vedas] to be known through a defective instrument;
because, since no defect whatsoever is possible in the word itself, it must be stated that the cause of error and so forth is exclusively a defect in the person.

Furthermore, if the relationship between words and their meanings were created by a person, then error and the like—which depend upon that [relationship]—would necessarily transfer even to the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) of the meaning of a sentence, which is caused by the knowledge of word-meanings derived from that [relationship].
Or else, the Veda itself would be of human origin.

In that regard, as for the relationship between words and their meanings—which consists in the nature of the signified and the signifier and is inseparable from the act of denotation—all such relationships are understood from another source.
By the maxim "like worldly convention," because [the Veda] is known in its own form and possesses beginningless continuity, it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

Likewise, since the meaning of the Veda is supersensible (*alaukika*), it is impossible for there to be a knowledge of an author regarding a sentence concerning that subject along with its source; therefore, the Veda is not of human origin.
If the Veda were also of human origin, then [one would have to rely on] those who are omniscient through the power of yoga, or on the Lord (*īśvara*) who is omniscient by nature.

Furthermore, since there is no distinction in the validity of their knowledge, and it is impossible to state any difference between those two [the Vedic and non-Vedic] words, they would necessarily be equal to the Smṛtis of Manu and others.
But surely— the Veda is of human origin, because it consists of sentences, like the sentences of Kālidāsa and others.
Thus, how can the Veda not be of human origin, given this inference, the observation of designations such as "the Kaṭhaka," and the Śruti text, "The three Vedas were born"?
And this is logical;

otherwise, since the dissolution (pralaya) established by the Mantras and Arthavādas exists, the Vedas would have perished at that time along with their students. Consequently, because it would be impossible to acquire the Mantras and Arthavādas, there would arise the contingency that knowledge [of them] could not occur, just as it cannot for other objects.
Therefore, just like the creation of other things, the Veda must also have a person as its author.
