For this very reason, since it is established in common worldly experience that the intention (*tātparya*) of a sentence uttered by a speaker consists in its being directed toward whatever cognition the speaker intended while uttering it, there is no need to postulate the existence of indicators such as the beginning and the conclusion (*upakrama-upasaṃhāra*) to determine the intention residing in the Vedic sentences.

Furthermore, since the validity of the knowledge arising from words depends upon the reliability of the speaker's statement, it follows that there is no possibility of invalidity for the knowledge produced by words.

Moreover, if the designation *samākhyāna* is accepted as being based on "proclamation" (*pravacana*)—as favored by the proponent of the established view (Siddhāntin)—then, because such proclamation is common to even wicked persons, the impossibility of an exclusive designation remains exactly as it was.
Therefore, the Veda is indeed of human origin.

If it is argued that even if this were so, since it is stated [in the Gītā] that "the conduct and tradition of those who know that," the Smṛtis would not attain equality with the Veda merely on the basis of being composed by those who know the Veda, we say:

no. For if they were of human origin, their validity as human statements would depend upon the conviction regarding their author; and since the author, whose form must necessarily be remembered, is invariably not remembered, there is the cognition of his non-existence.
Nor does the fact that the *Yoni* text, well-known among the Chāndogas, has a remembered author entail its being of human origin.

If the Sāman were of human origin, it would be established as being of non-human (apauruṣeya) origin precisely because its attainment occurs through the very recitation of the *uttara* and *ūha* texts; for otherwise, the scriptural injunction "if [it is] on the *yoni*, he sings it on the two *uttaras*" would result in being rendered purposeless.

Furthermore, the inference based on the reason of "being a sentence" is also inconclusive (*aprayojaka*), as it is characterized by a limiting condition (*sopādhika*)—namely, that it must be rooted in another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)—since this is likewise the case with sentences of human origin.
Because the meaning of the Veda cannot be grasped through direct perception,

statements such as "the three Vedas were born" are merely explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) serving as supplements to injunctions— such as "the Ṛgveda is recited aloud, the Yajurveda in a whisper, and the Sāmaveda aloud"— and thus do not constitute valid authority regarding their own literal sense. Furthermore, if these [statements] were dependent upon an agent [to complete the ritual], then, like an explanatory passage that makes known the nature of heaven required by the injunction for one desiring heaven, this too would be authoritative regarding its own sense by virtue of establishing an agent required by the injunction.
This is not the case;
by this, the proof of creation and dissolution from the mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) is refuted,
because even they lack authority regarding their own literal meaning since they are supplementary to other injunctions.

Furthermore, the designations such as *Kāṭhaka* and others are justified by some exceptional excellence in the teaching [of the text] by Kaṭha and his followers, or because it is possible for them to have been studied by the Kaṭhas through traditional succession (*paramparā*). Nor does it follow that the designations such as *Mānava* must also be based on teaching, which would imply that the *Smṛtis* and other such works are likewise [based on Vedic revelation].

Because those [Vedic hymns] have as their primary purpose the recollection of their authors— by means of the firm recollection of the authors in the form of the recitation of the lists of names from beginning to end—

for this very reason, even the recollection of the author in every sentence, such as "The *sūktas* of Vasiṣṭha are the seerly [work] of Viśvāmitra," is justified merely by the sight of the seers at the time of creation and so forth, due to the recollection of their vision and so on; thus, it is not by such a method that one can maintain that they have Vasiṣṭha and others as their authors.
Furthermore, because designations such as "Kāṭhaka" and so forth must be accounted for;

and because even though [the Veda] is not produced by an author, it is possible for the Veda to possess the nature of *tātparya* (purport) in the form of being for the sake of that which a sentence intends to convey—namely, that a sentence is directed toward whatever its cognition aims at—and thus it is improper to claim that such [purport] is untenable in the Veda;

and because all the factors constituting validity, such as the capacity to communicate meaning and the capacity to communicate an unknown object, are possible in the Veda as well, such validity is established even in the absence of being produced by the words of a trustworthy person (*āpta*).
Granted that the accounts of creation, dissolution, and the destruction of the Vedas are based on authoritative sources such as explanatory passages (arthavāda);
nevertheless, since saṃsāra is beginningless, it is more reasonable to assume that the Lord, being omniscient, teaches the Veda—which had arisen in one kalpa—in another kalpa.
Since this assumption is simpler, it is improper to postulate a new composition in every kalpa, which would involve unnecessary complexity; thus, the theory of the Lord's authorship is not tenable.
For if saṃsāra were to have a beginning, the creation of a new sequence would necessarily be logical;
indeed, if saṃsāra had a beginning, one would necessarily have to accept the creation of a new sequence.
Yet that is not possible.

Because the Vedas did not exist prior to creation, there would be an absence of dharma and adharma—which are knowable through the Vedas alone—and consequently, an absence of their performance; thus, the arising of pleasure and pain for living beings produced in another kalpa would be untenable.
Furthermore, since the composition of sentences is observed to be preceded by produced knowledge, it would entail the undesirable consequence of attributing produced knowledge to the Lord.
Moreover, because eternal knowledge would depend on the authority of the Vedas for its establishment, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya).

"Given that the Veda is authoritative, the Lord's authorship of it is established by virtue of His possessing eternal knowledge as revealed by it; and conversely, the authority of the Veda is established by virtue of His being its author.
By this [it is shown that] the earth and so forth have an agent.

The argument that the authority of the Veda is established by its being rooted in the knowledge of God— God being proven through the inference "because [the world] is an effect," and thus possessing eternal knowledge— is refuted;

for even by that much, since only a creator of the earth and so forth who possesses non-eternal knowledge is established, the authority of his knowledge cannot be proven without a foundational source of valid cognition (*mūla-pramāṇa*).
Therefore, even the Śruti text, "Whose exhalation is the Veda," declares that the Veda is established without effort, like a mere breath;
for the Veda is perceived as being uncreated, precisely because its author is not remembered.

Although the Veda—which consists of phonemes qualified by a specific sequence—is eternal insofar as the nature of the phonemes themselves is eternal, it is nonetheless non-eternal with respect to its specific sequence, since that sequence is produced by the causal complex of its utterance.
And since there exists some kind of sequence belonging to that same class at the time of creation, its eternity is established as being due solely to its beginninglessness in the form of its effects—

not, like the ether (*gagana*) and so forth, due to beginninglessness in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). This being the case, and since no cause for invalidity can possibly exist, it is entirely logical that the two previously mentioned characteristics of *dharma* and *adharma* are established through the very possibility of the arising of an uncontradicted cognition from [the Veda], which is inherently free from defects.
